title: IAM Roles & Temporary Credentials 🎭
description: Let AWS services or external identities assume permissions securely.

slides.title: What is an IAM Role? 🎭
slides.content:
# An Identity You Assume, Not Own

Unlike a user, a **role** doesn’t have permanent credentials (no password or access keys). Instead, you **assume** the role to get temporary security credentials.

Roles are used by:
- **AWS Services**: EC2 needs permissions to read from S3 – you assign a role to the instance.
- **Cross‑account access**: Another AWS account can assume a role in your account.
- **Federated users**: Corporate credentials (SAML, OpenID) can assume a role, avoiding creation of IAM users.

**Analogy**: A role is like an actor’s costume. The actor (user/service) puts on the costume and temporarily gains the costume’s permissions.

quizData.question: What is the key difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?

options.text: Users are free, roles cost money
Users have permanent credentials; roles provide temporary credentials when assumed
Roles can only be used for EC2

quizData.explanation: Roles don’t have long‑term keys or passwords. They issue short‑lived credentials via AWS STS when assumed.

slides.title: Trust Policy: Who Can Assume the Role 🤝
EC2 Instance Profile 🖥️
slides.content:
# Giving EC2 Permissions

You can’t directly attach a role to an EC2 instance. You create an **instance profile** – a container for the role – and attach that to the instance.

The AWS CLI and SDKs on the instance automatically retrieve temporary credentials from the instance metadata service. No hard‑coded keys needed!

> This is a major security win: never store AWS credentials on an EC2 instance.

slides.title: ⚠️ Credential Expiry
slides.content:
## Temporary Credentials Rotate

The credentials obtained by assuming a role are short‑lived (1‑12 hours). Applications must handle refreshing them. The AWS SDKs do this automatically.

slides.title: Pro Tip: Cross‑Account Roles Are Gold 🌉
slides.content:
## Avoid Creating IAM Users for Partners

If another AWS account needs access to your resources, create a role with a trust policy allowing their account. They can assume it without you managing their passwords. Much safer.
